# Abstract {.unnumbered}

<!-- RAP 2 (tax rates), findings in chapter order; adapted from the JMP abstract (JMP/paper.qmd). Previous version: Thesis/feedback/thesis-abstract-intro-archive-250926.md -->

Sales and value-added taxes that credit purchases reward firms for overreporting their inputs: every fictitious dollar of deductible inputs lowers their tax liability, and the higher the rate, the larger the reward. How this evasion responds to the tax rate is largely unknown, because true inputs are not observed and firms that overreport may be mistaken for low-productivity firms. This thesis separates overreporting from productivity using the production function, with corporations, which government and market scrutiny keep from evading, as the truth-reporting benchmark. The approach needs only reported inputs and output, so it applies equally to standard firm-level surveys and administrative data; I apply it to Colombian manufacturing firms from 1981 to 1991. First, a statistical test that remains valid under any detection probability and cost of evasion that vanish without evasion, and under any common production technology, and whose rejections can only point to overreporting, detects overreporting in 9 of the 18 industries liable for the sales tax, including 4 of the 5 largest, and in neither exempt industry. Second, deconvolution recovers its distribution: in the 7 industries where the test rejects at the 1 percent level, firms overreport on average 14.5 percent of their true materials in the median industry. Third, failing to correct for overreporting yields output elasticities of materials that are consistently larger, and productivity distributions that are more dispersed and less persistent: in the median industry, the 90–10 ratio is 66 percent larger and the half-life of productivity shocks is 52 percent shorter. Fourth, after a 1983 reform raised the sales-tax rate in most industries, overreporting by unincorporated firms in the affected industries rose by about 9 percentage points of true materials between 1983 and 1987. Finally, a structural model of detection and evasion costs shows that claimed deductions rise more than one-for-one with the purchases-side rate: a 1 percent increase raises them by about 1.2 percent, 0.2 points of which come from firms overreporting more, and the response to cuts is smaller. Undetected overreporting costs about 4 percent of the sales tax these firms owe on their sales.
